_comment: Storyboard for the Grade 4 Computing unit lecture film, Lesson 3 Sub-routines. Rendered by tools/create-ehel-unit-lecture.js. See lecture-video/BRIEF.md. Every beat is one narration clip; art.at names the phrases a picture waits for, and the page refuses to load if a phrase is not in its beat's say. The chapters follow LESSON[lecture] in order (decomposition; the main algorithm; following a call; written once used many times; changed in one place and shared). THE SAME-THING CLAIM IS THE KIT'S, NOT THE FILM'S: the 'Following a call' chapter builds its ribbon of finished steps from ART.algo.subExpand(main, subs) - the lesson's own expansion rule, mirrored in _rules.py - so the five-line main algorithm and the steps it ends up doing cannot disagree with the lesson. No count is spoken, because the lesson's own 'twenty steps' line does not match the steps it lists (see the film's report).
title: Sub-routines
subtitle: Grade 4 Computing
objectives: Understand that decomposition is a process that is used to break tasks into different parts (sub-routines).
Know how to use decomposition to break tasks into different parts, represented as algorithms.
Follow and understand algorithms that use a sub-routine.

beats.say: Getting ready for school is a big job. Break it into named parts.
Each part is a sub-routine: a small algorithm with a name.
A big task is easier in parts. Here is one: a school morning.
Decomposition breaks it into four parts: wash, dress, breakfast and bag.
In an algorithm each part becomes a sub-routine with a name.
A sub-routine is a small algorithm. WASH is face, teeth and hair.
It skips nothing. All the steps are still there.
The main algorithm is the short list at the top.
It has one line for each part, in the order they happen.
The first line is do WASH. Then do DRESS, do BREAKFAST and do BAG.
Then leave the house. That is five lines you can read at a glance.
Each do is a call. A call runs the sub-routine with that name.
Behind those five lines sits all the detail, tucked away.
Now follow it. You reach do WASH, so jump into that sub-routine.
Do every one of its steps: face, then teeth, then hair.
Then jump back to the line after the call, and carry on.
The next line is do DRESS, so jump in again: shirt, trousers, socks, shoes.
Back once more, on through BREAKFAST and BAG, then leave the house.
Five lines did every step in the parts. Nothing was skipped.
Bedtime has a main algorithm too: pyjamas, do WASH, do STORY, lights off.
There is do WASH again. The same sub-routine, in a different routine.
Both lists point at the same box of steps, written out only once.
It is called in the morning, and called again at bedtime.
One copy of the steps. Two calls to it. That is what reuse means.
Now add flossing to the WASH sub-routine, and watch both routines.
Both of them get flossing, and you edited neither of them.
You change one list, not three. That is three chances not to miss one.
Sub-routines share the work too. One person writes WASH.
Another writes DRESS, and the main algorithm joins them.
Decomposition breaks one big task into smaller named parts.
Each part is a sub-routine, and the main algorithm calls them in order.
A call jumps into a sub-routine. A return brings you back.
Written once, used many times, and changed in one place.
